title: Kinowo worker — JVM & pipeline diagnostics (k3s)

panels.title: Uptime (hours) — drops mark restarts
panels.description: (now − process_start_time)/3600. Every drop to ~0 is a restart of the worker process. A regular cadence is the tell for an OOM cycle rather than a deploy — deploys are irregular and carry a purple Deploy marker. The worker is a k3s pod now, so the reason lives in `kubectl -n <ns> describe pod` (look for OOMKilled) and `kubectl logs --previous`, not in `flyctl machine status`.

panels.title: CPU breakdown — centi-cores (process / JIT / GC)
panels.description: The worker's own CPU, split three ways: total process, the slice spent JIT-compiling, and the slice spent in GC (100 = one full core). GC climbing toward the process line is the SerialGC full-GC thrash signature — heap pressure, not work. JIT should be a burst after every restart and near-zero afterwards; a JIT line that never settles means the process keeps restarting. There is no credit-breakeven line any more: that was a property of Fly's shared-cpu billing, and this worker now has a whole k3s node's cores available. Note the host's CPU on the fleet dashboard will always read higher than this — k3s itself runs there too.

panels.title: Heap used against -Xmx
panels.description: Healthy is a sawtooth with a flat floor, comfortably under the cap. A floor that rises collection after collection is a heap leak; a sawtooth whose peaks graze the cap means the next reprojection will thrash SerialGC. The cap is plotted from jvm_memory_max_bytes rather than written into this text, so it stays right when -Xmx is retuned.

panels.title: Resident set size (RSS) against the pod cgroup limit
panels.description: Two readings of the same number: process_resident_memory_bytes (the JVM's process exporter) and kinowo_worker_process_rss_bytes (VmRSS, read from /proc/self/status by the vitals sampler that also computes the off-book gap below). They should lie on top of each other — drawn together so the gap panel's arithmetic is checkable rather than taken on faith. THE CEILING IS THE POD'S OWN cgroup memory limit, from kube_pod_container_resource_limits, per country (pl/uk/es 1Gi, de 1.5Gi, us 2Gi) — this is the number the kernel OOM-kills against, not the node's RAM. It replaced the Fly machine's ~960MB limit, and was blank for a while when nothing exported a pod limit. Read the SLOPE as well as the distance to the line: a steady climb that resets only at a restart is the native working set growing, and the uptime panel will show you the restarts it ends in.

panels.title: Native memory by NMT category (committed)
panels.description: Native memory HotSpot admits to committing, by NMT category — the buckets jvm_memory_* cannot see. This is where a non-heap leak shows itself: one category climbing steadily while the others stay flat names the culprit. Flat everything while RSS climbs means the growth is off-book (see the gap panel below), which is a different diagnosis entirely. Requires the JVM to be started with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary; if this panel is empty, that flag is missing rather than the memory being fine.

panels.title: Off-book native memory — RSS minus NMT-committed
panels.description: kinowo_worker_native_offbook_gap_bytes: RSS minus everything HotSpot admits to committing. Neither of the panels at the top of this dashboard can show it — jvm_memory_* covers the heap, the NMT panel covers the committed native categories, and this is the remainder. It is the primary signal for the ~5-6h non-heap OOM restarts: the 2026-07-09 probe found every NMT category flat across a whole 5h life while RSS climbed ~26MB/hr, which is glibc malloc retention/fragmentation in the C heap and appears here and nowhere else. READ THE SLOPE, NOT THE LEVEL — the level is normally NEGATIVE (around −200 to −320MB in steady state) because committed is not resident: pages can be committed and never touched. That is why this axis is deliberately not floored at zero. A gap climbing steadily toward and past zero, resetting only at a restart, is the pre-OOM signature; Pair it with the RSS panel above: that one shows the absolute number climbing, this one shows that the climb is NOT accounted for by anything the JVM reports.

panels.title: Direct & mapped buffer pools
panels.description: NIO buffers the JVM allocates outside the heap — the HTTP client's read buffers live here. Sitting beside the NMT and off-book panels because it is the one native consumer with a named, per-pool reading: 'used' growing without bound while the NMT categories stay flat points at buffers never being released, typically a response body left unread. Steady state is a small, flat direct pool.

panels.title: JVM threads (current / peak)
panels.description: Live and peak JVM thread count. A count that climbs without bound ends in an 'unable to create native thread' OOM and is a thread leak; a stable count means the memory problem is somewhere else. Peak sitting far above current after a quiet period is normal — it is a high-water mark, not a live reading.

panels.title: Read-model projection — avg duration (ms), compute vs write
panels.description: Per-call cost of the read-model projection, split into its two phases: COMPUTE (project, solid) is resolve/synopsisByCity/ratings before any write; WRITE (write-burst, dashed) is writer.upsertMovie/diffScreenings once the variants are known — one document per (card, city, cinema), sequentially. A wide release's write phase running long while compute stays flat points at the write loop (city count, Mongo round-trips), not at enrichment — on 2026-09-08 a UK release took up to ~40 minutes to reach all 73 of its cities with no signal telling compute, write and change-stream delivery apart; this pairing is that signal. A 3-5x inflation of EITHER at a FLAT call rate = the daytime GC-thrash flare (projection is a victim of GC pauses, not the cause). · READS ZERO, NOT BLANK, WHEN NOTHING PROJECTED. This is rate(sum)/rate(count), which is 0/0 = NaN in any window where the projector did not run -- and Grafana draws a NaN-only series as "No data", which is indistinguishable from the panel being broken. The `or (... * 0)` term makes an idle projector an explicit zero line. A FLAT ZERO IS NOT NORMAL -- it means the projector has not run at all. The _count sitting at exactly 1 on every worker is the SEED observation WorkerTaskMetrics makes at boot to materialize the series, not a projection: 1 is the reading for never-projected. This panel read flat zero for hours on 2026-08-29 while the Mongo migration had left every change stream dead (an invalidated resume token that nothing cleared and nothing reopened), and that flatness was the only visible symptom -- the read model was taking prune deletes and no upserts. Read a flat zero here against kinowo_worker_movie_change_events_total: zero events while the pipeline is plainly working means the STREAM is down, not that the projector is idle.

panels.title: Resolution cache — hit rate % by source
panels.description: Share of identity resolutions (film → TMDB id / IMDb id / rating-site url) served from cache instead of running a live probe chain. A chain costs up to ~30 upstream GETs for RT/Metacritic and ~36 for Filmweb, so this is the cache's actual saving. Low here means the cache is doing little — the resolved url is persisted on the film record anyway, which is the competing gate.

panels.title: Resolution chains RUN — by source and kind
panels.description: Probe chains actually executed, per second. `miss_resolved` mints a cached answer and should decay as the corpus resolves; `miss_unresolved` is a chain that found nothing and — because the cache is hits-only — was NOT cached, so the same film burns the same chain again next cycle. If miss_unresolved dominates, the fix is caching negative results, not deleting the cache.

panels.title: Durable-store share of cache hits % by source
panels.description: Of the hits, how many came from the Mongo `resolve_*` collections rather than the in-process Caffeine layer. This is what the durable half buys over a plain in-memory cache — it is the only part that survives a worker restart. Near 0% across sources means the 5 collections + TTL-index reconciliation are carrying nothing and could be dropped.

panels.title: GC — collections per second by collector
panels.description: How often each collector runs, per country. Young ('Copy') climbing with a flat old-gen line is normal churn; 'MarkSweepCompact' climbing is the shape that precedes a heap-exhaustion death, and pairs with the GC centi-cores line on the CPU panel.

panels.title: Cinema-scrape HTTP outcomes — error share, scrape phase (per country)
panels.description: A failure-budget view scoped to phase="scrape": ONLY the cinema-site HTTP — every listing scrape, chunk scrape and per-film detail fetch — with the third-party metadata/rating/resolution APIs (phase="enrich") excluded; its companion enrich-phase panel below covers those. Each error band's thickness is that error's share of scrape attempts, stacked at the floor; the empty space above is the clean remainder. This isolates cinema-scrape health from the enrichment APIs' by-design 404 slug-probing and API 429s: here a rising http_403 (a cinema Cloudflare/datacentre-IP block) or http_5xx/timeout stands out instead of hiding under the enrichment 404 noise floor. The 'requests/s' line on the right axis exists so an empty chart is never ambiguous: a healthy requests line with no error areas means the phase is running clean, whereas a flat zero requests line means the phase has stopped making calls at all — a completely different problem that an error-share panel alone would hide as 'no data'.

panels.title: Enrichment HTTP outcomes — error share, enrich phase (per country)
panels.description: The scrape panel's companion, scoped to phase="enrich": ONLY the third-party metadata/rating/resolution APIs (TMDB/IMDb/RT/Metacritic/Filmweb/Letterboxd/Wikidata/Cinemeta), with cinema-site scraping (phase="scrape") excluded. Each error band's thickness is that error's share of enrich attempts, stacked at the floor; the empty space above is the clean remainder. Reading this side on its own: a large steady http_404 band is EXPECTED — the RT/Metacritic resolvers probe up to 4 candidate slugs per title and the wrong ones 404 by design — while http_401 (a bad/missing API key) or a rising http_429 (an API rate-limiting us) is the signal to watch. Improbable codes (409/422/451/…) fold into the residual http_4xx; other categories: http_5xx=server, timeout=connect/read, connection_error=refused/DNS/reset/TLS, other=unclassified. The 'requests/s' line on the right axis exists so an empty chart is never ambiguous: a healthy requests line with no error areas means the phase is running clean, whereas a flat zero requests line means the phase has stopped making calls at all — a completely different problem that an error-share panel alone would hide as 'no data'.

panels.title: Intern pool — occupancy against its cap
panels.description: StringPool collapses the byte-identical SourceData strings a film repeats across its per-cinema slots (one 'action', not the 66,106 copies a worker-us heap dump found). It is BOUNDED, and that bound fails SILENTLY: past the cap Caffeine evicts, the next lookup of an evicted value allocates a fresh String, and interning degrades to a no-op that still costs a hash per call. No error, no log -- just a heap that grows. MEASURED 2026-09-03 the pool sits at 28,695 of 131,072 on the US corpus (22%) and the vocabulary SATURATES -- US has 3x the UK's slots and barely more distinct strings -- so a line here should rise to a plateau near a fifth of the cap and stay there. Pinned AT the cap would be new: that is the corpus outgrowing the pool, and then the cap is the thing to raise. The cap is plotted rather than written into this text so it stays right when it is retuned.

panels.title: Intern pool — evictions and hit ratio
panels.description: The two halves of 'is the pool still paying for itself'. evictions_total flat at zero is a pool doing its job, and at 22% occupancy it should be exactly that -- any sustained climb is thrash, strings interned and immediately thrown away, so duplicates reach the heap anyway. hit_ratio is the share of lookups served an instance the pool already held: high is healthy, and a FALL alongside rising evictions is the degradation itself rather than a symptom of it. Note neither says anything about strings that never reach the pool -- interning happens only at MovieCache.buildCinemaSlot, so a rehydrate through MovieCodecs allocates fresh instances that these gauges will never see. Both are process-level (one pool per JVM, shared by every country's wiring), so neither carries a country label.

panels.title: Caches — entries, and the count bound where there is one
panels.description: Entry counts for every registered cache, and the maximum for the one actually bounded by count (`task_dedup`). `movie_corpus` has NO maximum and that is deliberate: it is the hydrated corpus rather than a working set, and publishing a zero maximum would render as '100% full' on any ratio and invent an alarm. For it the shape is the signal — a count that tracks the country's corpus is healthy, one that climbs past it has stopped evicting. There are no byte series here because no cache in this JVM is weighed in bytes: the venue detail cache was, and was deleted once nothing read it (the TTL now expires inside the DetailEnrich refresh window, so a scheduled refresh can never be served from cache).

panels.title: Caches — hit ratio and evictions
panels.description: The two halves of 'is this cache paying for itself'. On `task_dedup` a high hit ratio is the point: every hit is a Mongo enqueue round-trip not made, so a FALL alongside rising evictions is the dedup being evicted and those round-trips coming back. On `movie_corpus` a hit is a Mongo read not made; it is unbounded, so its eviction line sits at zero by construction rather than by luck, and a climb there would mean something has started bounding it. Both are per-country — one wiring per country in the one JVM.

panels.title: TTL indexes that disagree with the code
panels.description:
`kinowo_worker_ttl_index_mismatches` — TTL indexes whose `expireAfterSeconds` does not match the constant in the code AND which the app could not rebuild. ZERO IS THE ONLY HEALTHY VALUE.

WHY THIS IS WORTH A PANEL. `createIndex` cannot ALTER a TTL index and `readWrite` does not carry `collMod`, so for years a change to a TTL constant reached Mongo only if the collection had never been indexed — every other change was rejected into a `logger.debug` nobody reads. It cost a real defect: `detailCache-cinema-city` was still reaping at 6h on 2026-09-06, a day after the code moved it to 2h, which made half that chain's scheduled refreshes re-derive what they already had and stamp it as fresh.

THE EXPENSIVE FAILURE IS AN INDEX THAT IS NOW ABSENT. The reconciler drops and recreates, so a drop that succeeded and a create that failed leaves the collection reaping NOTHING and growing without bound — check `detailCache-*` and `uptimeBuckets` sizes first. WHICH collection is in the worker log, not in this series (a per-collection label would vanish when healthy, and an alert cannot tell an absent series from a healthy one): `kubectl -n kinowo logs deploy/worker-pl | grep -i 'TTL index'`.

panels.title: Scrape depth/breadth guard verdicts — reject vs accept, by country
panels.description: ScrapeHealth's two per-tick guards (services.movies.ScrapeHealth.depth / .breadth), reject=a tick looked depth- or breadth-degraded and was held; accept=the guard gave up after enough consecutive rejections and let the smaller board land. `healthy` isn't drawn — it's the overwhelming default and this panel is about the exceptions. A `reject` rate that never returns to zero is a cinema (or several) stuck failing the same way tick after tick — check RemovalAudit's [scrape-depth]/[scrape-prune] logs for which one. A run of `accept`s on one axis, one country, is either a real sustained schedule cut or a scraper that's been degraded in the same shape for hours (Kino Aurum, 2026-09-13: a breadth-guard deadlock — 57 accumulated slot-keys against an 11-film board — that had been silently re-triggering every ~2h for days before anyone noticed, purely from log-reading; this panel is what would have shown it on day one).

panels.title: Scrape writes silently skipped — by country and reason
panels.description: A scrape observed a title this tick but its write did not land, and neither reason throws or logs an ERROR on its own: cache-miss-race is MovieCache.putIfPresent returning false because a concurrent rekey of some OTHER title invalidated this key between the read and the compute (ScrapeLanding's own comment on `landed` names the mechanism); unreadable-row is the cache-miss branch finding the stored row could not be read at all (pairs with a WARN log naming the film). Both are already handled safely downstream (the title is spared that tick's prune, nothing is deleted) so a low, occasional rate here is not an incident — but a SUSTAINED nonzero rate for one country is a title whose corpus data has stopped updating without any exception ever being thrown, which is exactly the shape that made the still-open Kino Aurum screenings-freeze investigation (2026-09-13) take a multi-hour Mongo forensics session instead of a five-second look at this line.

panels.title: Read-model heals vs the stream's card retirements, by country
panels.description:
`kinowo_worker_readmodel_heals_total` (bars, left): ready rows the 30-min prune sweep (trigger=sweep) or the boot check (trigger=boot) re-projected because the read model lacked one of their cards or venues. ZERO IS THE HEALTHY READING: every heal is a row the change-stream path should already have written, and the site served without it until the sweep came round. Sweep heals are alerted by ReadModelHealsRecurring (read-model-projection.rules); boot heals are not.

`kinowo_worker_readmodel_cards_retired_total` (lines): cards the change-stream path removed on its own, by reason. The pair is the diagnosis: a `row-unready` retirement rate that the heals trail by a sweep is a row flapping out of readiness and back (the 2026-09-11..23 TMDB re-try defect: ~500 row-unready retirements and ~26 heals a day, visible until now only in WARN lines). Heals with no matching retirements point at a missed stream event instead (a slot written after the row's last projection). The worker's heal WARN lines name the row ids.

Each point counts ITS OWN interval (at least 30 min, one prune sweep), not a trailing half hour, so one burst is one bar. Boot heals and `row-deleted` retirements land right after a worker deploy by design: the boot check runs before the change stream resumes, and UnscreenedCleanup's daily pass runs 20 s after every boot. A mass boot heal is what a change to the projected ids looks like (2026-09-23 18:22: the Polish re-cluster moved every screening onto a new city page, 376 rows re-projected once); only boot heals that recur deploy after deploy are a defect.

panels.title: Change-stream apply — oldest unapplied event's wait, and how many are waiting
panels.description:
The APPLY half of the three change-stream cursors (the delivery half is `kinowo_worker_change_stream_last_event_age_seconds`). Every delivered event is handed to ONE apply thread (a stitch read, then the synchronized read-model projection); `kinowo_worker_change_stream_apply_lag_seconds` (lines, left) is how long the oldest event still waiting there has waited since delivery, recomputed per scrape so a stuck apply climbs in a straight line; `kinowo_worker_change_stream_apply_pending` (dashed, right) is how many are waiting, bounded by each cursor's demand window (256).

HEALTHY is a flat line at or near zero with humps of SECONDS. The three cursors share that one thread, so a burst on one delays the other two and their lines rise TOGETHER. The humps are scrape waves: each venue scrape that changes a film's showtimes re-projects the WHOLE film, and a wide US film (thousands of slots) takes up to ~2s to project (p99 of `kinowo_worker_readmodel_project_duration_seconds`), so a dozen queued behind a Regal/AMC wave, or behind the scrape wave a worker starts ~2 min after boot, reads as 5-12s (US, 2026-09-23). Both lines are the worst sample in each step (`max_over_time` over `$__interval`, min interval 1m): a hump usually lasts ONE 30s scrape, and the raw gauge showed it or dropped it depending on the zoom. Why it exists: until 2026-09-23 the resume token was saved at DELIVERY, so a restart skipped every event still waiting here and nothing showed how many that was. Alerted by ChangeStreamApplyLagging (over 10 minutes, for 10 minutes).

panels.title: TMDB re-try resolves that landed on a queued resolve — upgraded or not
panels.description:
`kinowo_worker_resolve_retry_duplicates_total`: a re-try resolve (mode=retry-miss, the scheduled unresolved re-try; mode=force, the operator's re-enrich) whose film already had a ResolveTmdb task queued under the same dedupKey. upgraded = the WAITING task now searches in the re-try's mode or above (raised to it, or already there); not-upgraded = the queued task was already being worked on with its old mode, so this re-try's search did not happen.

Why it exists: until 2026-09-23 every one of these was DROPPED by the queue's dedup, visible only as `tasks_enqueued{result=deduped}` — indistinguishable from a harmless duplicate plain resolve — and the plain resolve then stopped at the remembered miss the re-try existed to look past, for another 24h. A sustained not-upgraded rate means re-tries keep arriving while their film is mid-resolve. Panel only; no alert.

panels.title: Side rows under venues the roster no longer lists, by country
panels.description:
`kinowo_worker_retired_venue_side_rows` (lines): `screenings` / `movie_slots` rows filed under a venue name missing from the country's roster (RetiredVenueCensus: at boot, hourly, and right after each cleanup run; id-only reads). `kinowo_worker_retired_venue_future_showtimes` (bars, right): the upcoming showtimes on those screenings rows. ZERO IS HEALTHY.

Dropping a cinema stops its scrape and the read path ignores its rows; the daily RetiredVenueRows cleanup deletes a screenings/slot pair once BOTH twins are older than its 24h grace, so a freshly dropped venue sits here for up to about two days (before that cleanup existed, Kino Etiuda OBK's rows stayed for days). A foreign country's venue here means rows landed in the wrong database. Alerted by RetiredVenueRowsLingering (above zero for 50h: the cleanup's 24h grace plus its daily tick) — the watchdog for the retired-venue cleanup.

panels.title: Venue pairs sharing their programme, by country and scope
panels.description:
`kinowo_worker_duplicate_venue_pairs`: pairs of roster venues whose upcoming (film, start time) programmes are (nearly) the same (DuplicateVenueCensus, off the 5-min corpus scan), by scope. scope=same_city: two venues of one city overlapping by 90%+ of the larger programme — one screen listed twice under two names, or two venues wired to one upstream listing, which the name-based offline roster audit cannot see. scope=cross_city: two venues sharing no city, 20+ showtimes each, at 95%+ — one venue's feed listed under another's name (Flicks once gave Syracuse IN's Pickwick the Park Ridge IL one's). Venues under 5 upcoming showtimes are skipped. A pair whose shared showtimes book through each venue's own links (chain-mates: Cineworld, Phoenix Theatres, Caribbean Cinemas run one grid estate-wide) is two venues and is not counted; the same session on another host, or a venue with no links, still counts. Pairs on `services.cinemas.roster.DistinctVenuePairs` are cleared. ZERO IS HEALTHY.

The worker's WARN line "duplicate-venue census (<country>, <scope>)" names the pairs whenever the set changes. Two real venues programmed alike with no booking links to tell them apart go on DistinctVenuePairs with the reason. Alerted by DuplicateVenueListing (above zero for 24h).

panels.title: Share of cinema scrape checks that FAILED (not empty), by country
panels.description:
Failed cinema uptime checks (fetch or parse threw) over all cinema checks — failed + succeeded + parsed-but-empty — in the last 30 minutes, from the web tier's `kinowo_uptime_recent_failures` / `_successes` / `_zeroes` gauges, cinema services only (enrichment sources, the per-venue `|enrichment` and chain-wide `<Chain> Enrichment` detail rows, hosts, image proxies and the residential proxy excluded -- the same exclusion CinemaScrapeFailureShareHigh reads through). An empty listing is a closed venue, not a failure, so it only ever dilutes this share.

Normal p99 over 14 days: de 0.10, es 0.06, us/uk 0.02, pl 0.17. The PL ~0.30 and UK 0.75-0.95 excursions from 09-18 evening to 09-21 this panel once drew were Cineworld Enrichment detail fetches, not scrapes, until the chain-wide rows were excluded on 2026-09-24. Alerted by CinemaScrapeFailureShareHigh (over 20% for 2h, at least 10 checks). A single venue failing every attempt is CinemaScrapeOldestAgeHigh's job instead. Gapped, not zeroed, when a country made no checks.

targets.expr: sum by (country) (kinowo_uptime_recent_failures{country=~"$country", service!~"IMDb|TMDB|Filmweb|Metacritic|Rotten Tomatoes|Residential proxy|.* Enrichment|img: .*|[a-z0-9.-]+\\.[a-z]{2,}|.*\\|enrichment"}) / (sum by (country) (kinowo_uptime_recent_failures{country=~"$country", service!~"IMDb|TMDB|Filmweb|Metacritic|Rotten Tomatoes|Residential proxy|.* Enrichment|img: .*|[a-z0-9.-]+\\.[a-z]{2,}|.*\\|enrichment"} + kinowo_uptime_recent_successes{country=~"$country", service!~"IMDb|TMDB|Filmweb|Metacritic|Rotten Tomatoes|Residential proxy|.* Enrichment|img: .*|[a-z0-9.-]+\\.[a-z]{2,}|.*\\|enrichment"} + kinowo_uptime_recent_zeroes{country=~"$country", service!~"IMDb|TMDB|Filmweb|Metacritic|Rotten Tomatoes|Residential proxy|.* Enrichment|img: .*|[a-z0-9.-]+\\.[a-z]{2,}|.*\\|enrichment"}) > 0)

panels.title: Read-model venues per projection — rebuilt vs reused, by country
panels.description: `kinowo_worker_readmodel_venue_projections_total{outcome}`: the screenings rows a projection considered, counted per interval (at least a minute), so a boot's burst of rebuilds is one bar rather than one smeared across every overlapping window. rebuilt (bars, right axis) = the venue's slots (showtimes or link) moved since its row was written, or this process never wrote it (every venue after a worker boot, when the memo is seeded from the read model and cannot vouch for the inputs). reused (lines, left axis) = the row was already written from identical inputs, so it was neither built nor rewritten. A showtime change at one venue of a wide release reads 1 rebuilt against thousands reused — that skip is what took the ~2 s per-film re-projection off the single change-apply thread (panel 28). Rebuilt tracking reused one-for-one outside a boot means the input hash is missing its matches: every projection is rebuilding the whole film again.

panels.title: Staging newcomer kicks — rows decoded per kick, and kicks per min
panels.description: `kinowo_worker_staging_newcomer_kick_rows_total / kinowo_worker_staging_newcomer_kicks_total`: how many staging rows the StagingReaper decoded each time a StagingNewcomerDiverted kicked a film's chain. A kick is due only for a film NEW to staging, so its group is that venue's own row(s) and the line sits near 1 (a few when venues land the same new film concurrently). Until 2026-09-23 every venue JOINING an incubating film kicked too, and the k-th of N venues decoded k rows: rows/kick of ~N/2 -- ~1,220 for the presale staged at 2,441 US venues, which took the US scrape tick from 27s to 1,419s. A line climbing with a wide release's venue count is that quadratic back; StagingNewcomerKickReadsWide fires on it. Kicks/min (dashed, right axis) is the denominator: a ratio over a handful of kicks is noise. Reads ZERO, not blank, while nothing is being kicked.

panels.title: Repository writes that FAILED — by country, collection, op and exception
panels.description: `kinowo_worker_repository_write_failed_total`: a movies / movie_slots / screenings / pending_movies write that THREW (every Mongo repository write goes through services.movies.RepositoryWrite). ZERO IS THE HEALTHY READING. Each failure is also a WARN line naming the film, and the cache rolls the row back so the next identical scrape retries the write — so a short blip heals itself, while a sustained line is a write that keeps failing (a codec that cannot encode a field, a validator, a full disk). Alerted by RepositoryWritesFailing (worker-pipeline.rules). Added 2026-09-24: a codec bug failed 34 upserts over ~6h with nothing counting it, and two new films never reached the site until a restart. The exception label is the class's simple name. Every known collection/op is seeded at 0 for the expected exception classes, so the first failure shows; any other class appears on its first failure and shows from its second.

panels.title: Share-card directory — bytes on disk vs the budget, by country and kind
panels.description: `kinowo_worker_share_cards_bytes{kind}`: everything in the country's share-card directory on k3s-worker-1 -- rendered cards (`kind="card"`), the poster cache (`kind="poster"`) and the card bases (`kind="base"`), temp files included -- against `kinowo_worker_share_cards_budget_bytes` (KINOWO_SHARE_CARD_BUDGET_MB, 1 GiB by default), which covers all three TOGETHER. `current` (`kinowo_worker_share_cards_current_bytes`) is the part no pruner may delete: the card, base and poster of every film web_movies points a card at. The janitor evicts the rest oldest-first every ten minutes once the total passes the budget. ShareCardsNearBudget fires on the total above 85% for 30m; ShareCardsOverBudget when current alone exceeds the budget. Gauges are read from the directory, so every replica reports the same number: `max`, never `sum`. Files per kind are on the right axis.

panels.title: Share-card coverage — films on screen whose card for their current inputs exists
panels.description: `kinowo_worker_share_cards_coverage_ratio`: of the films with screenings in web_screenings, the share whose card for their CURRENT inputs exists on disk -- one card per film, drawn in the deployment's language, from any of its current poster candidates. Published by the backfill tick every minute from its daily sweep. Films that left the screens since the sweep drop out of the ratio as their cards retire, so it no longer sags overnight. A drop after a template bump or a ratings refresh is the re-render queue working through it; a line that stays low while the render counter is quiet is the backfill not running. ShareCardCoverageLow fires under 95% for 6h (a fresh backfill refills in under 3h); ShareCardCoverageAbsent when a worker is up without this gauge for 1h.

panels.title: Share-card renders per interval — by outcome and reason, and how each was drawn
panels.description: `kinowo_worker_share_cards_render_total{outcome,reason}`: render tasks by result (each logged by the worker as `share card: <filmId> "<title>" <outcome> — <reasons>`, a details change naming its part, e.g. `details(synopsis)`) -- rendered, existing (another task or replica already wrote it), rendered_no_poster (every poster failed: a card without one, re-tried daily and at each worker boot), failed (the card could not be drawn at all; ShareCardRendersFailing fires above 25% of at least ten renders per 30m, for 30m) -- and by WHY: new_film (the first-publish gate), backfill (a card out of date whose layout changed before the worker last booted, so it cannot say which part), or the card input that moved (poster = the poster the card was drawn from left the film's candidates; title, year, ratings at displayed precision, language, template, details = genres/director/synopsis/host). A re-render that moved several inputs counts once per input. A ratings wave after a rating refresh is expected (measured ~242 rating-driven changes a day fleet-wide); a steady `details` line is synopsis churn re-rendering cards. Dashed, right axis: `kinowo_worker_share_cards_render_path_total{path}` -- base_hit = the card drawn as its cached base (the card without its badges, q95 4:4:4 under `.base/`) plus the badges, which is what a ratings change costs (~28 ms against ~54 ms for a rebuild, measured locally); base_rebuild = the base redrawn from the cached poster after any non-rating change; full = a posterless card drawn whole.

panels.title: Share-card deletions — by kind and reason
panels.description: `kinowo_worker_share_cards_pruned_total{kind,reason}`: files deleted. Each film has at most three -- its card, base and poster, each overwritten in place by a re-render, so nothing is ever superseded. retired = the files of a film dropped from the read model (at once, by the projection) or off the screens (the daily prune); budget = evicted oldest-first to get under the budget; temp = an abandoned write older than the one-hour grace. Nothing younger than an hour is ever deleted, and no file of a film web_movies points a card at. The daily prune's burst, just after 03:00 UTC (or five minutes after a boot that finds that day's prune never ran), is normal; a steady budget line means the directory lives at its budget.

panels.title: Poster cache — hits and misses, and how the misses' fetches went
panels.description: `kinowo_worker_share_cards_poster_cache_total{result}`: a render found one of the film's posters already cached (hit, no download) or had to fetch (miss). `kinowo_worker_share_cards_poster_fetch_total{result}` (dashed, right axis) is what each poster URL's download + shrink did on a miss: ok, or failed (unreachable, over the 50 MB cap, or undecodable) -- a failing primary beside a working fallback is one failed URL but no failed film. ShareCardPosterFetchFailing counts FILMS instead (`kinowo_worker_share_cards_poster_load_total`: did any candidate work) and fires when more than half of at least ten fail for 30m. Hits dominating after the backfill is the cache doing its job: only a changed poster URL costs a fetch. A failed fetch names why in `reason` (http_4xx, http_5xx, timeout, network, too_large, empty_body, decode_error, vips_cap = the vips child hit its memory cap, progressive_estimate = refused by the JPEG-header estimate before decoding, encode_error), and the worker logs `share card: poster for <film> from <host> failed: <reason>` (INFO at most once a second). A film none of whose posters work still gets a card, drawn without a poster (render outcome `rendered_no_poster`), which the daily backfill re-tries.

panels.title: Facebook re-scrapes of film pages — sent, failed, rate-limited
panels.description: `kinowo_worker_share_cards_rescrape_total{outcome}`: requests to the Graph API asking Facebook to re-scrape one film page, so a cached preview shows the film's current card. A film is queued (a) when it was published without its card (the first-publish gate timed out) and finally gets one, and (b) when the card of a film in its first week changes. Every country's worker drains ONE fleet-wide queue (the facebook_rescrapes collection of the shared fleet database) on ONE quota: one request every 20 s on average across the whole fleet (never two closer than 15 s), whichever country sends it, each page on its own. sent = accepted; failed = refused, that page alone retried with back-off (1, 2, 4, 8 min) and dropped after 5 attempts; rate_limited = Facebook named its rate limit, and the whole fleet waits an hour; disabled = a film asked for with no FACEBOOK_APP_ID / FACEBOOK_APP_SECRET or no fleet database, so nothing is queued. The worker log names each refusal with Facebook's own code and message. Before 2026-09-26 re-scrapes were per-country tasks sending all of a film's city pages back to back — the 2026-09-25 16:20 spike of ~680 HTTP 403s was one film in 265 US and 63 UK cities.

panels.title: Facebook re-scrapes waiting — film pages queued, by country
panels.description: `kinowo_worker_share_cards_rescrape_waiting`: pages each country has waiting in the fleet's re-scrape queue. At one request per 20 s fleet-wide the queue drains ~180 pages an hour, so a burst (a film showing in hundreds of cities, a template change re-drawing every recent film) shows as a ramp that falls over hours. Flat and non-zero for over an hour = the fleet is holding for Facebook's rate limit (see rate_limited on the panel to the left). A backlog that is no smaller than it was three to four hours ago, for another hour, pages as ShareCardRescrapesNotDraining.

panels.title: Documents skipped as UNDECODABLE — by country, process and collection
panels.description: `kinowo_worker_decode_failures_total` and `kinowo_web_decode_failures_total`: documents a read-model full scan (web_movies / web_screenings) SKIPPED because they could not be decoded. ZERO IS THE HEALTHY READING. The skip keeps one corrupt document from sinking the keyset page it arrived in, but each skipped document is a film or screening that process serves or projects without; the WARN line names its _id ("skipping undecodable document"). Alerted by DocumentsUndecodable (worker-pipeline.rules). Added 2026-09-24: the skip used to be a log line and nothing else.

panels.title: Env-gated alerters and integrations — 1 wired, 0 switched off by a missing env var
panels.description:
`kinowo_worker_alerter_enabled{alerter}` (the in-app Telegram alerters: Filmweb fallback, Filmweb drops, staging stuck) and `kinowo_worker_integration_enabled{integration}` (TMDB, OMDb, the residential proxy, Zyte, Sentry, the Facebook re-scrape). ONE IS THE ONLY HEALTHY VALUE.

WHY THIS IS WORTH A PANEL. Each of these is wired as `Env.get(...)` in a for-comprehension, so a missing secret becomes a `None` and the feature is simply not there -- no error, no log line. When the workers moved from Fly to k3s the Telegram chat ids were left behind and all three alerters were off for weeks with nothing noticing. WHICH key is missing is in the worker's boot log: `kubectl -n kinowo logs deploy/worker-pl | grep 'is OFF: missing'`. `WorkerAlerterDisabled` / `WorkerIntegrationDisabled` (worker-pipeline.rules) fire after 30 minutes at 0.

panels.title: Identity shadow run — resolver clusters by relation to the pipeline's films
panels.description: `kinowo_worker_identity_shadow_films`: the identity resolver's SHADOW run (ShadowIdentityReaper, docs/design/identity-resolver.md §8), after each settle tick, from the observation store alone — no external lookups. Its clusters by relation to the films today's pipeline made of the same listings: identical (same listings, same TMDB film), split (part of one pipeline film), merged (listings of two or more), moved (same listings, another film). Serves nothing; the diff behind it is in `identity_shadow_diff`, the decisions on /admin/identity. Series exist only for countries with KINOWO_IDENTITY_SHADOW on. Panel only; no alert.

panels.title: Identity shadow run — family crossings and resolve seconds
panels.description: `kinowo_worker_identity_family_crossings`: constraint edges that crossed a family in the last shadow resolve. ZERO IS HEALTHY — a crossing means a rule was added without its block key; the resolve is refused and the previous run stays the latest (the worker logs "identity shadow: resolve refused"). `kinowo_worker_identity_resolve_seconds`: how long the last resolve took (seconds per corpus, measured offline in docs/design/identity-resolver.md §15).

description: Why a worker is misbehaving, once the application-health dashboard has told you that one is. There are FIVE workers — pl, uk, de, us and es, each its own k3s Deployment — so every panel is scoped by the Country variable and carries the country in its legend; pick one to isolate it, or All to compare. Memory (heap, NMT native categories, the off-book gap, buffers, and the pod's real cgroup limit from kube-state-metrics), CPU split by JIT and GC, GC frequency, restarts, resolution-cache hit rates, and the error shape of the outbound HTTP the scrape and enrichment phases depend on. All from each worker's own /metrics on k3s via local-prometheus. There is no CPU-credit panel: shared-CPU credit was a Fly billing concept and the whole throttle path it drove was deleted on 2026-09-04, so no series behind it exists. · NOTE (2026-08-29): this fleet was built today. The oldest metric on it is about 6h old and the app metrics are younger still — the DE and UK workers are under an hour, and the web tier's HTTP metrics about an hour. A window longer than a series has existed draws a gap, which is indistinguishable from a broken panel. The default range is set to match what the data can actually show; raise it as history accumulates.
